articles.headlineTranslated: QIAGEN presents new data on the efficacy of QuantiFERON in tuberculosis prevention.
articles.summary: QIAGEN reports data on QuantiFERON-TB Plus (QFT-Plus) efficacy for preventing TB as of 19 March 2026. In a BMC Public Health study of HIV-positive adults in Thailand, QFT-Plus screening reduced the modeled lifetime risk of developing active TB by 41% versus the tuberculin skin test (TST) and lowered lifelong health costs. Findings support earlier, more precise TB infection detection enabling timely preventive treatment and more efficient resource use across settings. The report cites a growing evidence base: over 2,500 published studies validating QuantiFERON and more than 125 million QuantiFERON-TB tests performed worldwide, including high-risk groups such as those on immunosuppressive therapies. Nadia Aelbrecht, VP and Head of Infectious Diseases at QIAGEN, emphasizes QuantiFERON’s reliability for detecting TB infections to guide prevention.

articles.headline: QIAGEN Highlights Newly Published Data Supporting Efficacy of QuantiFERON for TB Prevention
articles.summary: As of 2026-03-19, a BMC Public Health study in Thailand among adults living with HIV finds TB infection screening with QuantiFERON-TB Plus (QFT-Plus) reduces modeled lifetime risk of progression to active TB by 41% versus tuberculin skin test (TST) and lowers lifetime healthcare costs. The data support earlier preventive therapy by improving detection of latent TB infection, enabling more efficient resource use. The QFT-Plus program is backed by a large evidence base—over 2,500 published studies and about 125 million QuantiFERON-TB tests used worldwide, including populations at higher risk of reactivation such as those on immunosuppressive therapies. Nadia Aelbrecht of QIAGEN emphasizes reliability and applicability across settings to guide preventive treatment in clinicians, laboratories, and public health authorities.

articles.summary: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) receives new clinical and health economic support for TB infection detection, especially in immunocompromised and high-risk populations. A BMC Public Health study among adults living with HIV in Thailand shows QFT-Plus lowers modeled lifetime risk of progression to active TB by 41% versus tuberculin skin test and reduces lifetime healthcare costs, enabling earlier preventive therapy. Globally, over 2,500 studies and more than 125 million tests support QFT-Plus; WHO estimates about 10 million people develop active TB annually. QIAGEN marks World TB Day 2026 with a CPD-accredited online program on March 24, 2026. The company is pursuing fifth-gen QFT, AI-enhanced risk prediction, and automation with Diasorin for high-throughput testing to strengthen TB detection and prevention.

articles.summary: TB testing with QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) demonstrates advantages in detecting Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections, especially among immunosuppressed individuals and other high-risk groups. A BMC Public Health study in adults with HIV in Thailand found that QFT-Plus, compared with the tuberculin skin test (TST), reduced the modeled lifetime risk of developing active TB by 41% and lowered total lifelong healthcare costs. The data add to a large evidence base—over 2,500 studies and more than 125 million QuantiFERON tests worldwide—supporting early preventive treatment. Ahead of World TB Day on March 24, 2026, QIAGEN hosts an online CPD-accredited program with international TB experts. The company also advances a fifth-generation QFT, explores AI to predict progression risk, and expands automation via Diasorin LIAISON systems for high-throughput TB testing. TB remains a leading global killer, with about 10 million cases annually.

articles.headlineTranslated: Ministry of Public Health reiterates that meningococcal disease in Thailand is found sporadically, not spreading as a cluster outbreak like England.
articles.summary: Thailand reports sporadic meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis) with no cluster outbreak, unlike England. By 19 March 2026, 5 cases have occurred since the start of 2026, across Nan, Yala, Nonthaburi, Nakhon Si Thammarat, and Udon Thani (1 each); 3 deaths (case fatality 60%); incidence 0.008 per 100,000. No epidemiological links among cases. Over the past decade (2015–2024), Thailand shows a low burden, averaging 20–30 cases annually and no large outbreaks. The disease spreads via droplets or prolonged close contact, notably in dormitories, educational settings, or camps. Symptoms include abrupt high fever, neck stiffness, drowsiness, and purpuric rash; urgent medical evaluation is advised. For travelers to group settings, vaccination should be considered at least 10 days before travel. Ongoing surveillance and rapid response—early recognition, diagnosis, treatment, contact tracing, and risk communication—are essential.

articles.headlineTranslated: Ministry of Public Health assures 'meningococcal disease' in Thailand is found sporadically, not spreading as a cluster outbreak like England; surveillance continues.
articles.summary: Meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis) in Thailand remains sporadic, with 5 laboratory-confirmed cases and 3 deaths (case fatality 60%) since the start of 2026, across Nan, Yala, Nonthaburi, Nakhon Si Thammarat, and Udon Thani (one case each). No epidemiological links identified; national status is not a cluster outbreak, unlike a recent England cluster. Age distribution centers on 0–4 years, followed by 40–49 and 20–29 years. Over the past decade (2015–2025), Thailand reported low incidence (roughly 20–30 cases/year) without large-scale outbreaks. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets/contact, with higher risk in dormitories, schools, and camps. Clinical signs include high fever, neck stiffness, altered consciousness, and purpuric/petechial rash. Public health guidance emphasizes rapid detection, diagnosis, prompt treatment, contact tracing, and risk communication. Vaccination consideration before travel to high-density settings (at least 10 days prior) is advised; follow official health advisories for updates.

articles.headline: Heading to Bali, Vietnam or Thailand? Why a measles vaccine is more important than ever
articles.summary: Measles outbreaks persist in Bali, Vietnam, and Thailand, prompting Australian authorities to stress vaccination ahead of travel. From Jan 2025 to Mar 2026, Australia recorded 60 measles infections: 34 acquired overseas and 26 locally acquired; 18 linked to an imported case, eight with no clear source, indicating community transmission. Indonesia ranked third in CDC’s outbreaks by Feb 2026; measles is endemic in Thailand, with rising activity in Vietnam. Measles spreads by airborne particles up to two hours and is contagious from four days before to four days after rash. Early flu-like symptoms precede a rash; complications include pneumonia, otitis media, and encephalitis; fatality about 1–3 per 1,000 in high-income settings. Herd immunity around 95%. In Australia, 2024 first-dose at 12 months was 94.7% and 18-month second-dose 89.5%. Vaccination, including a six-month infant dose for travelers, should be at least two weeks before departure.

articles.headlineTranslated: SPCOM. Department of Disease Control–Bangkok moves forward with proactive tuberculosis case finding and screening in communities to speed patients’ access to treatment | Daily News
articles.summary: Tuberculosis (TB) proactive case finding expands in Bangkok. The SPCOM (Institute of Urban Disease Prevention) and Bangkok Metropolitan Administration are screening crowded communities in Bang Kha Laem District under the Bangkok Urban Slum TB Screening Project (2024–2026). The program covers 85 slum communities (≈63,433 residents) with chest X-ray screening and sputum testing; confirmed TB cases are registered for treatment and followed until cure. From 2024–2025, 52 communities were screened, 3,575 chest X-ray assessments identified 15 TB cases, with ongoing follow-up for treatment and household contacts; 33 more communities are planned for March–July 2026. Globally, WHO reports TB as the leading infectious killer, with about 10.7 million new cases and 1.23 million deaths annually. Thailand in 2025 was projected to have ~104,000 new TB cases and 11,300 deaths, with 81,703 diagnosed and registered and an estimated 22,297 undiagnosed in high-risk groups. Symptoms include chronic cough (>2 weeks), possible hemoptysis; transmission is airborne. The initiative aims to speed diagnosis, reduce transmission, and end TB in Thailand by 2035 (2578).

articles.headlineTranslated: Meningococcal disease situation in Thailand in 2026: 5 cumulative cases, 3 deaths.
articles.summary: Thailand's Epidemiology Division reports five cumulative meningococcal disease cases (Neisseria meningitidis) in 2026, with three deaths (case fatality rate 60%), data as of 18 March 2026. No outbreak; sporadic cases across Nan, Yala, Nonthaburi, Nakhon Si Thammarat, and Udon Thani (one in each). Peak age 0–4 years, followed by 40–49 and 20–29. Ten-year trend shows about 20–30 cases per year; current activity is low but meningococcal disease remains highly severe with rapid progression and high mortality risk. Key measures: intensified surveillance, rapid diagnosis and antibiotics, contact tracing with prophylaxis, risk communication. Symptoms prompting care: fever with neck stiffness, drowsiness, or purpuric rash. Travelers to crowded settings should seek medical advice if concerned.

articles.headline: Heading to Bali, Vietnam or Thailand? Why a measles vaccine is more important than ever
articles.summary: Measles outbreaks persist in Southeast Asia, Bali, Vietnam, and Thailand, as of February 2026. Australian health authorities warn overseas travel drives cases, with New South Wales reporting 60 infections in 2025–26; 34 acquired overseas, 18 linked to a known imported case, eight with no clear source. Indonesia remains a major source and ranks third in the CDC’s outbreak list; Vietnam shows rising activity and Thailand remains endemic, with transmission up since 2023. Measles is highly infectious via airborne particles and can spread from four days before to four days after rash onset. Herd immunity around 95% is needed. In Australia, first-dose coverage reached 94.7% by age 12 months in 2024, second-dose 89.5% by 18 months. The National Immunisation Program provides free vaccines at 12 and 18 months; a 6-month early dose is available for traveling infants. Adults born 1966+ without two doses should consider vaccination. Two doses protect about 99%.

articles.headline: Scientists Found Evidence of the Black Plague in a 4,000-Year-Old Sheep
articles.summary: Yersinia pestis DNA was detected in 4,000-year-old domesticated sheep remains from Arkaim, a Bronze Age settlement in the southern Ural mountains on the Russia-Kazakhstan border, marking the first non-human genome recovery of the plague bacterium. The team's findings, published in Cell, add a livestock vector dimension to Bronze Age plague spread, alongside earlier evidence that the bacterium lacked the Yersinia murine toxin, which would have aided flea infection. That earlier work suggested transmission via airborne droplets, contaminated food, or bodily fluids. The Sintashta culture's large herds and horse riding could have driven wide geographic reach across Eurasia. Although the discovery helps explain plague DNA found thousands of kilometers apart, a natural reservoir remains unidentified, with candidates including rodents on the Eurasian steppe or migratory birds. The article notes that plague, while suppressed, still challenges public health lessons from history.

articles.headlineTranslated: This summer, Disease Control Office 12 Songkhla warns that rabies infection can be fatal; scratches or bites from animals—seek medical attention promptly; recommends following the guidelines.
articles.summary: Rabies in Songkhla Province, Thailand: The 12th Disease Control Office warns the infection can be fatal. Scratches or bites from animals require prompt medical care. Rabies virus is transmitted from warm-blooded animals, mainly dogs and cats, but other species can carry it. Incubation is typically 15–60 days (some cases under 10 days or over a year). Early symptoms include headache, fever, sore throat, malaise, and itching at the wound site; advanced signs include agitation, photophobia, hydrophobia, swallowing difficulty, seizures, paralysis, coma, and death within 2–7 days after onset; once neurological symptoms appear, mortality is essentially 100%. Prevention follows three principles: (1) vaccinate pets (initial at 2–4 months; boosters at 6–12 months and annually); (2) avoid bites using the five 'Y' rules; (3) post-exposure care—wash wound 10–15 minutes, apply antiseptic, seek vaccination, and observe the animal for 10 days. If the animal dies, test for rabies. Hotline 1422.

articles.headlineTranslated: High-end enterovirus vaccines officially enter overseas markets, launching operations and undergoing a structural upgrade.
articles.summary: Vietnam grants drug license for Taiwan’s High-End Vaccine enterovirus vaccine (6547), marking the first overseas approval and enabling exports to Vietnam, with plans to expand into ASEAN. Since its August 2023 Taiwan debut, the enterovirus vaccine has sold over 500,000 doses and held a market share above 95%. The Vietnamese license is partnered with Substipharm Biologic; Singapore licensing is under application, with further targets including Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines. To meet rising demand, two existing production lines will be repurposed for enterovirus vaccine production, with annual capacity exceeding 1 million doses. A 2026 investment of 870 million yuan funds a third biotech building; completion is expected in 2027, followed by equipment installation, 2028 efficacy-batch production authorization, and full-scale production in 2029, signaling strong ASEAN growth potential.

articles.headlineTranslated: High-end enterovirus vaccine secures drug approval in Vietnam.
articles.summary: Vietnam grants drug approval for High-end's enterovirus 71 (EV71) vaccine, marking the first EV71 vaccine to receive local market authorization and a milestone for Taiwan-originated vaccine exports. The product, submitted in 2023, targets Vietnam's newborn population—about 1.36 million births per year—and addresses a vaccine gap, as no EV71 vaccine is currently available there. With approval, High-end aims to enter the Southeast Asia vaccine market and has signed a regional distribution deal with French firm Substipharm Biologics to develop markets in Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. To secure supply for ongoing demand, the company is building a vaccine production line at Zhubei's third biotech campus, planning about NT$871 million in capex to support the existing EV71 vaccine and next-generation products. EV71 is one of the most dangerous enteroviruses for infants and is prevalent in the Asia-Pacific region, with Southeast Asia projected to require millions of doses long-term.

articles.headline: Man discharged from hospital after SFTS diagnosis: Taiwan CDC - Focus Taiwan
articles.summary: Taiwan CDC reports a man in his 70s from northern Taiwan discharged after a severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) diagnosis, Taiwan's third domestic case. He sought care in late February for fever and weakness and was hospitalized over two weeks before release. The infection source remains under investigation. SFTS is mainly transmitted by tick bites, though human-to-human spread is possible. Nine contacts have been identified and are monitored through March 26; none have symptoms. Environmental sampling found no ticks inside or on pets; 16 ticks outside were negative for SFTSV. Taiwan previously reported domestic SFTS cases in 2019 and 2022. SFTS first emerged in China in 2009 and has since been reported in Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, Myanmar and Thailand. Symptoms include fever, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite; severe disease can cause multiple organ failure and death, with a 5–15% fatality rate.

articles.headlineTranslated: Check this out! The Department of Disease Control warns about three diseases and two health hazards commonly found during the summer season.
articles.summary: Thailand’s Department of Disease Control warns of increased summer illness in 2026 from three water/foodborne diseases and two heat-related hazards. Group 1: digestive tract and water diseases: diarrhea from contaminated food/water, food poisoning from toxins in foods (e.g., mushrooms, seafood), and cholera from contaminated sources. Prevention centers on the mantra 'eat hot, cook fresh, clean': cook thoroughly, avoid shared utensils, wash hands with soap and water or sanitizer, drink clean or boiled water from sealed containers, and use ice from certified plants. Group 2: heat-related illnesses: heat rash, heat cramps, heat exhaustion, and heat stroke, risk higher for the elderly, chronically ill, and outdoor workers. Advice: limit outdoor activity, hydrate 8–10 cups daily, wear breathable clothing, avoid alcohol. Heightened drowning risk March–May; follow water safety, use life jackets, observe lifeguards, and supervise children and the elderly. 12 regional offices and SRRT are mobilized; hotline 1422.

articles.headlineTranslated: Man in northern Taiwan contracts Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS); tick captured near home; source of infection under investigation.
articles.summary: Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) confirmed in a man in his 70s in northern Taiwan, the country’s third domestic case. He developed weakness in late February with fever; at admission he had leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and liver/kidney dysfunction. After isolation and treatment, he defervesced and recovered; two PCR tests were negative and he was discharged after about two weeks. Infection source remains under investigation; a tick near his home and 16 ticks collected outside were identified as hard ticks but not Haemaphysalis longicornis, the main SFTS vector, and none tested positive for the virus. Nine close contacts and healthcare workers are under monitoring; none symptomatic. Environmental assessment on March 12 found rodent traces but no captured mice. Monitoring continues to March 26. Taiwan previously reported domestic SFTS cases in 2019 and 2022. Internationally, SFTS has been reported in China since 2009 and in Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Myanmar, and Thailand.

articles.headlineTranslated: China Again! Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome: Only 3 Cases in Taiwan, Taiwan CDC Says Fatality Rate as High as 30%
articles.summary: Taiwan’s CDC reports one locally acquired Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) case in a northern Taiwan man in his 70s with no recent international travel. He developed weakness in late February, was admitted for fever and thrombocytopenia, and SFTS was lab-confirmed on March 2; discharged March 16. Since 2019, Taiwan has three domestic SFTS cases (2019, 2022, 2026). The fatality rate may reach 30%. Internationally, China reported SFTS in 2009; Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, Myanmar, and Thailand have since reported cases; East Asia shows expansion. SFTS is mainly transmitted by tick bites; human-to-human spread in healthcare is rare. Incubation 7–14 days; symptoms include fever, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, cytopenias; severe cases can involve multi-organ failure. No antiviral therapy; prevention emphasizes avoiding tick habitats and protective clothing, DEET/picaridin. Environment around home yielded 16 ticks (not Haemaphysalis longicornis) and 44 rodent traps; risk remains.

articles.headlineTranslated: The Department of Disease Control warns the public to beware of three common diseases and two health hazards that often occur during the summer.
articles.summary: Thailand's Department of Disease Control warns of three food- and waterborne diseases and two summer hazards as 2026 hot season begins: diarrhea from contaminated food or water, food poisoning from toxins in foods or seafood, and cholera from contaminated sources, all causing watery stools and dehydration; cholera can be severe. Prevention: eat thoroughly cooked food, use clean utensils, wash hands before meals and after toilet, and drink clean boiled or bottled water with ice. Heat hazards include heat illness (rash, cramps, exhaustion, heat stroke) especially among the elderly, chronically ill, and outdoor workers. Avoid prolonged outdoor activity; hydrate (8–10 cups daily); wear breathable clothing; avoid alcohol. Drowning risk rises March–May, affecting children under 15 and adults. Follow water safety, wear life jackets, supervise, and use the 'Shout, Throw, Reach' rescue method; do not dive. Avoid alcohol during water activities; sites should have lifeguards and safety gear. Alerts were issued to 12 provincial offices and SRRT teams; hotline 1422 for inquiries.

articles.headline: Российские туристы массово отравились в отеле на Пхукете: чем опасен отдых в Таиланде
articles.headlineTranslated: Russian tourists poisoned en masse at a hotel in Phuket: what are the dangers of vacationing in Thailand
articles.summary: Mass illness among Russian tourists at MBC Condotel in Phuket, Thailand triggers a rapid health-safety review as Russia’s Rospotrebnadzor requests data from Thailand’s Ministry of Public Health. Over the past two weeks, guests report high fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and conjunctivitis; in one case a child developed purulent tonsillitis. No official cause is confirmed; travelers attribute symptoms to tap water described as cloudy with a foul odor. The investigation aims to assess epidemiological risks. experts warn Thailand’s tropical climate elevates risks for gastrointestinal infections and vector-borne diseases. Mosquito-borne threats may include chikungunya and dengue; first dengue infection is usually mild, but reinfection can cause severe dengue hemorrhagic fever. While Thailand is broadly epidemiologically favorable, the primary risk to tourists is unprocessed water—recommendations include carrying bottled water or boiling it, avoiding ice, and maintaining hygiene until sources and outcomes are clarified.
